# Preface {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning title="A work in progress"}
This book is a **work in progress**. It is still under development and will
keep growing and improving over time. Chapters may be revised, expanded, or
reorganized as it is used in the classroom; when something looks unfinished,
that is why. Questions and suggestions are welcome.
:::

**EDR|AI** — *Evidence-Driven Research in the Age of AI: How to Design,
Analyze, Verify, and Defend* — is an open research manual for undergraduate
students in economics, political science, business, and biology who want to
turn curiosity into credible, defensible, evidence-based insight in a world
where AI can produce almost everything. It was first written for an Honors
research seminar at Purdue University, and it is deliberately
institution-agnostic: any instructor or student, anywhere, is welcome to adopt
it.

Its one message: *AI is your arm and your research assistant, not your brain.*
You will direct AI tools through the
**Specify → Delegate → Interrogate → Inspect → Verify → Document → Defend**
workflow while keeping every research decision your own. One rule runs through
every verification step in this book (collected in the
[Verification Guide](verification-guide.qmd) appendix): **AI can review AI** —
a second model is a real auditor of the first — **but the last decision is
always human**.

**This book is also a manual you can follow to a finished project.** Every
chapter ends with an **It is your turn** section: concrete steps that apply the
chapter to your own research. Work them in order and they chain into a
complete, defensible research project — and by the last page, a draft research
artifact (a paper, note, or poster) with your name on it. You do not need to be
enrolled in any course for that to work; you need curiosity and the discipline
the book teaches.

Blair, Coppock and Humphreys' *Research Design in the Social Sciences* (RDSS,
free at [book.declaredesign.org](https://book.declaredesign.org)) is the theory
text that EDR|AI translates for the undergraduate audience. In the original
course the EDR|AI chapter is the **required** reading each week and the
matching RDSS chapters are **recommended** for depth. Each chapter names a
research decision, works an example, links a Colab lab, shows an AI failure and
how to catch it, and hands the work back to you.

The book has six parts: research when AI does "everything"; from curiosity to
research design; the research pathways (observational and experimental,
descriptive and causal, and prediction); producing credible evidence with AI;
communicating and defending research; and research after the conference.

**Languages.** EDR|AI is also available in
[Português (Brasil)](../book-pt/index.html) and
[Español](../book-es/index.html) — use the language links at the top of any
page to switch at any moment. The English edition is the source of truth; the
translations are regenerated from it as it evolves.

If your course runs the flipped format this book supports, most lectures are
led by a student: the day's **Student Research Lead**. That lead's brief lives
at the start of the corresponding lecture notebook, and the appendix
[The Student Research Lead](srl.qmd) collects the format, the preparation
cadence, and the expectations in one place. To meet the person behind the
book, see [About the Author](author.qmd).
